claim: The carboxysome is a bacterial microcompartment that assembles around many copies of the enzymes ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase and carbonic anhydrase to facilitate carbon fixation in cyanobacteria.
source: Such a process occurs during the formation of the carboxysome, a bacterial microcompartment that assembles around many copies of the enzymes ribulose 1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/ oxygenase and carbonic anhydrase to facilitate carbon fixation in cyanobacteria.
evidence: This is established knowledge about carboxysomes cited in the abstract.

claim: Two classes of assembly pathways lead to encapsulation of many-molecule cargoes: one where shell assembly proceeds concomitantly with cargo condensation, and another where cargo first forms a dense globule followed by shell protein assembly and budding.
source: Our simulations identify two classes of assembly pathways leading to encapsulation of many-molecule cargoes. In one, shell assembly proceeds concomitantly with cargo condensation. In the other, the cargo first forms a dense globule; then, shell proteins assemble around and bud from the condensed cargo complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational simulations described in the manuscript.

claim: Assembly can be tuned between the two pathways by modulating protein interactions.
source: the simulations predict intermediates and closure mechanisms not accessible in experiments, and show how assembly can be tuned between these two pathways by modulating protein interactions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the computational simulations varying interaction parameters.

claim: Viruses surround their genomes with a protein capsid.
source: For example, viruses surround their genomes with a protein capsid, while bacteria use large icosahedral shells known as bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) to sequester the enzymes and reactions responsible for particular metabolic pathways (Kerfeld et al., 2010; Axen et al., 2014; Shively et al., 1998; Bobik et al., 1999; Erbilgin et al., 2014; Petit et al., 2013; Price and Badger, 1991; Shively et al., 1973; Shively et al., 1973; Kerfeld and Erbilgin, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Bacteria use large icosahedral shells known as bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) to sequester the enzymes and reactions responsible for particular metabolic pathways.
source: For example, viruses surround their genomes with a protein capsid, while bacteria use large icosahedral shells known as bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) to sequester the enzymes and reactions responsible for particular metabolic pathways (Kerfeld et al., 2010; Axen et al., 2014; Shively et al., 1998; Bobik et al., 1999; Erbilgin et al., 2014; Petit et al., 2013; Price and Badger, 1991; Shively et al., 1973; Shively et al., 1973; Kerfeld and Erbilgin, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Within diverse bacteria, BMC functions have been linked to bacterial growth, carbon fixation, symbiosis, or pathogenesis.
source: Within diverse bacteria, BMC functions have been linked to bacterial growth, carbon fixation, symbiosis, or pathogenesis (Kerfeld and Erbilgin, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Carboxysomes are large (40–400 nm), roughly icosahedral shells that encapsulate a dense complex of the enzyme ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RuBisCO) and other proteins to facilitate the Calvin-Bensen-Bassham cycle in autotrophic bacteria.
source: Carboxysomes are large (40–400 nm), roughly icosahedral shells that encapsulate a dense complex of the enzyme ribulose-1,5-bisphosphate carboxylase/oxygenase (RuBisCO) and other proteins to facilitate the Calvin-Bensen-Bassham cycle in autotrophic bacteria (Price and Badger, 1991; Shively et al., 1973; Shively et al., 1973; Iancu et al., 2007; 2010; Kerfeld et al., 2010; Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior literature.

claim: Genomic analysis suggests that many BMCs with diverse functions assemble via similar pathways.
source: Genomic analysis suggests that many BMCs with diverse functions assemble via similar pathways (Cameron et al., 2013; Kerfeld and Erbilgin, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The factors determining which assembly pathway occurs are unknown.
source: The factors determining which of these assembly pathways occurs are unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: The structure of the cargo can strongly influence assembly pathways and products in viral capsid assembly.
source: Previous experimental and theoretical studies of encapsulation by icosahedral shells, e.g. the assembly of viral capsids around their nucleic acid genomes (e.g. Hu and Shklovskii, 2007; Kivenson and Hagan, 2010; Elrad and Hagan, 2010; Perlmutter et al., 2013; 2014; Mahalik and Muthukumar, 2012; Zhang et al., 2013; Zhang and Linse, 2013; Hagan, 2008; Devkota et al., 2009; Dixit et al., 2006; Borodavka et al., 2012; Dykeman et al., 2013; 2014; Zlotnick et al., 2013; Johnson et al., 2004; Patel et al., 2015; Cadena-Nava et al., 2012; Comas-Garcia et al., 2012; 2014; Garmann et al., 2014a; 2014b; Malyutin and Dragnea, 2013), have demonstrated that the structure of the cargo can strongly influence assembly pathways and products.
evidence: This is supported by extensive citations to prior literature.

claim: Changing the cargo topology from a nucleic acid to a fluid complex comprising many, noncovalently linked molecules leads to new assembly pathways and different critical control parameters.
source: However, BMCs assemble around a cargo which is topologically different from a nucleic acid — a fluid complex comprising many, noncovalently linked molecules. We demonstrate here that changing the cargo topology leads to new assembly pathways and different critical control parameters.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the computational simulations in the manuscript.

claim: Tunability of cargo loading is a key functional difference between the two classes of pathways.
source: We find that tunability of cargo loading is a key functional difference between the two classes of pathways.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation results.

claim: Shells assembled around a diffuse cargo can be varied from empty (containing almost no cargo) to completely full.
source: Shells assembled around a diffuse cargo can be varied from empty (containing almost no cargo) to completely full, whereas assembly around a condensed, procarboxysome-like complex invariably produces full shells.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation results.

claim: Assembly around a condensed, procarboxysome-like complex invariably produces full shells.
source: Shells assembled around a diffuse cargo can be varied from empty (containing almost no cargo) to completely full, whereas assembly around a condensed, procarboxysome-like complex invariably produces full shells.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation results.

claim: The encapsulated cargo becomes ordered due to confinement.
source: While we find that the encapsulated cargo becomes ordered due to confinement, complete crystalline order in the globule before encapsulation inhibits budding.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation results.

claim: Complete crystalline order in the globule before encapsulation inhibits budding.
source: While we find that the encapsulated cargo becomes ordered due to confinement, complete crystalline order in the globule before encapsulation inhibits budding.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation results.

claim: Icosahedral symmetry can accommodate at most 60 identical subunits.
source: Since icosahedral symmetry can accommodate at most 60 identical subunits, formation of large icosahedral structures requires subunits to assemble into different local environments.
evidence: This is established knowledge about icosahedral geometry.

claim: Formation of large icosahedral structures requires subunits to assemble into different local environments.
source: Since icosahedral symmetry can accommodate at most 60 identical subunits, formation of large icosahedral structures requires subunits to assemble into different local environments.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the constraint of icosahedral symmetry.

claim: The subunits in icosahedral structures can be grouped into pentamers and hexamers, with 12 pentamers at the icosahedron vertices and the remaining subunits in hexamers.
source: The subunits can be grouped into pentamers and hexamers, with 12 pentamers at the icosahedron vertices and the remaining subunits in hexamers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about icosahedral structures.

claim: Recent AFM experiments demonstrated that hexamers are the basic assembly unit during the assembly of BMC shell facets.
source: Recent AFM experiments demonstrated that hexamers are the basic assembly unit during the assembly of BMC shell facets (Sutter et al., 2016), and the carboxysome major shell proteins crystallize as pentamers and hexamers (Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: The carboxysome major shell proteins crystallize as pentamers and hexamers.
source: Recent AFM experiments demonstrated that hexamers are the basic assembly unit during the assembly of BMC shell facets (Sutter et al., 2016), and the carboxysome major shell proteins crystallize as pentamers and hexamers (Tanaka et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The model considers two basic assembly units, one a pentamer and the other a hexamer, with interactions designed so that the lowest energy structure corresponds to a truncated icosahedron with 12 pentamers and 20 hexamers.
source: Motivated by these observations, our model considers two basic assembly units, one a pentamer and the other a hexamer, with interactions designed so that the lowest energy structure corresponds to a truncated icosahedron with 12 pentamers and 20 hexamers (Figure 1).
evidence: This describes the computational model design.

claim: For the simulated density of cargo particles, the phase behavior corresponds to a vapor at εCC=1.3.
source: For the simulated density of cargo particles, the phase behavior (in the absence of shells) corresponds to a vapor at εCC=1.3, liquid-vapor phase coexistence for εCC∈[1.6,2.0] (the phase coexistence boundary is slightly below εCC=1.6), and a solid phase at εCC=3.0.
evidence: This is determined from the simulation results.

claim: For the simulated density of cargo particles, the phase behavior corresponds to liquid-vapor phase coexistence for εCC∈[1.6,2.0].
source: For the simulated density of cargo particles, the phase behavior (in the absence of shells) corresponds to a vapor at εCC=1.3, liquid-vapor phase coexistence for εCC∈[1.6,2.0] (the phase coexistence boundary is slightly below εCC=1.6), and a solid phase at εCC=3.0.
evidence: This is determined from the simulation results.

claim: For the simulated density of cargo particles, the phase behavior corresponds to a solid phase at εCC=3.0.
source: For the simulated density of cargo particles, the phase behavior (in the absence of shells) corresponds to a vapor at εCC=1.3, liquid-vapor phase coexistence for εCC∈[1.6,2.0] (the phase coexistence boundary is slightly below εCC=1.6), and a solid phase at εCC=3.0.
evidence: This is determined from the simulation results.

claim: Tuning εCC through phase coexistence dramatically alters the typical assembly process.
source: We find that tuning εCC through phase coexistence dramatically alters the typical assembly process.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation results.

claim: Strong cargo interactions (εCC≥1.6) drive formation of a globule followed by assembly and budding of a shell, such as observed for β-carboxysomes.
source: Strong cargo interactions (εCC≥1.6) drive formation of a globule followed by assembly and budding of a shell, such as observed for β-carboxysomes (Figure 2A, Simulation Video 1), while under weak interactions (εCC<1.6) shell assembly usually proceeds in concert with cargo encapsulation (Figure 2B, Simulation Video 2), as suggested for assembly of α-carboxysomes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation results shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Under weak cargo interactions (εCC<1.6) shell assembly usually proceeds in concert with cargo encapsulation, as suggested for assembly of α-carboxysomes.
source: Strong cargo interactions (εCC≥1.6) drive formation of a globule followed by assembly and budding of a shell, such as observed for β-carboxysomes (Figure 2A, Simulation Video 1), while under weak interactions (εCC<1.6) shell assembly usually proceeds in concert with cargo encapsulation (Figure 2B, Simulation Video 2), as suggested for assembly of α-carboxysomes.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Near the phase boundary (εCC=1.6) a system of pure cargo particles is metastable on the timescales simulated.
source: Near the phase boundary (εCC=1.6) a system of pure cargo particles is metastable on the timescales we simulate.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: For εSC>4, adding shell subunits drives nucleation of a cargo globule with shell subunits adsorbed on the surface.
source: However, for εSC>4, adding shell subunits drives nucleation of a cargo globule with shell subunits adsorbed on the surface.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: For moderate interaction strengths (2.5≤εSS≤3.5) the globule grows to a large size, typically containing at least twice the cargo molecules that can be packaged within a complete shell.
source: For moderate interaction strengths (2.5≤εSS≤3.5) the globule grows to a large size, typically containing at least twice the cargo molecules that can be packaged within a complete shell.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: The complete shell contains 120–130 cargo particles, which is slightly above random close packing (≈120 particles) but below fcc density (≈150 particles).
source: The complete shell contains 120–130 cargo particles, which is slighty above random close packing (≈120 particles) but below fcc density (≈150 particles, see appendix 1.2).
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: Increasing the shell-shell interaction strength drives faster shell assembly and closure, thus limiting the size of the globule before budding.
source: Increasing the shell-shell interaction strength drives faster shell assembly and closure, thus limiting the size of the globule before budding.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: For the largest interaction strength simulated (εSS=4.5) the globule typically does not exceed the size of a single shell, and multiple globules nucleate within the simulation box.
source: For the largest interaction strength we simulated (εSS=4.5) the globule typically does not exceed the size of a single shell, and multiple globules nucleate within the simulation box (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: Multiple nucleation events were rare in the carboxysome assembly experiments.
source: This observation could place an upper bound on shell-shell interaction strengths, since multiple nucleation events were rare in the carboxysome assembly experiments (Cameron et al., 2013) (however, we discuss potential complicating factors within the cellular environment below).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to experimental studies.

claim: For εCC≥1.6 and εSS≤3, large values of the assembly order parameter (e.g. >32) are observed, which indicate formation of a large amorphous globule consistent with the procarboxysome precursor to carboxysome shell assembly.
source: For εCC≥1.6 and εSS≤3 we observe large values of the order parameter (e.g. >32, the red and yellow regions in Figure 4), which indicate formation of a large amorphous globule consisent with the procarboxysome precursor to carboxysome shell assembly (Cameron et al., 2013).
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results shown in Figure 4 and compared to experimental observations.

claim: For εCC=1.3 the cargo forms an equilibrium vapor phase in the absence of shell subunits.
source: For εCC=1.3 the cargo forms an equilibrium vapor phase in the absence of shell subunits.
evidence: This is determined from the simulation results.

claim: Above threshold values of εSS and εSC, the diffuse cargo molecules drive nucleation of shell assembly.
source: However, above threshold values of εSS and εSC, the diffuse cargo molecules drive nucleation of shell assembly.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: For low εSC, assembly captures only a few cargo molecules, leading to complete, but nearly empty shells.
source: For low εSC (Figure 2C), assembly captures only a few cargo molecules, leading to complete, but nearly empty shells.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results shown in Figure 2C.

claim: For larger εSC, the shell-cargo interactions drive local condensation of cargo molecules, and shell assembly and cargo complexation proceed in concert.
source: For larger εSC (Figure 2B, and Simulation Video 2), the shell-cargo interactions drive local condensation of cargo molecules. Shell assembly and cargo complexation then proceed in concert, resembling the mechanism proposed for assembly of α-carboxysomes (Iancu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Tuning the shell-cargo interaction dramatically affects cargo loading, with a sharp transition from empty to filled shells around εSC=2.
source: Thus, tuning the shell-cargo interaction dramatically affects cargo loading, with a sharp transition from empty to filled shells around εSC=2.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: The transition from empty to filled shells closely tracks the equilibrium filling fraction.
source: This transition closely tracks the equilibrium filling fraction (Figure 5C), measured by simulating a complete shell made permeable to cargo molecules.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing dynamics and equilibrium simulations shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Assembly of full shells (by either pathway) is typically about two orders of magnitude faster than assembly of empty shells.
source: Assembly of full shells (by either pathway, Figure 2A or Figure 2B) is typically about two orders of magnitude faster than assembly of empty shells (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is observed by comparing simulation timescales in Figure 2.

claim: Cargo molecules initially promote shell nucleation by stabilizing interactions among small, sub-nucleated clusters.
source: Cargo molecules initially promote shell nucleation by stabilizing interactions among small, sub-nucleated clusters.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing faster assembly with cargo.

claim: The presence of a condensed globule provides a large cross-section for adsorption of additional subunits, significantly enhancing the flux of subunits to the partial capsid, thus increasing its growth rate.
source: Then, the presence of a condensed globule provides a large cross-section for adsorption of additional subunits, significantly enhancing the flux of subunits to the partial capsid, thus increasing its growth rate.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing faster assembly with cargo.

claim: The condensed cargo particularly facilitates insertion of the last few subunits, which are significantly hindered by steric interactions.
source: The condensed cargo particularly facilitates insertion of the last few subunits, which are significantly hindered by steric interactions, as noted previously for simulations of empty virus capsids (Nguyen et al., 2007).
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results and supported by citation to prior work.

claim: The simple free energy model reproduces the threshold parameter values required for shell assembly with no adjustable parameters.
source: The simple free energy model (Equations (1–2)) reproduces the threshold parameter values required for shell assembly with no adjustable parameters (color map in Figure 3).
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the theoretical model to simulation results in Figure 3.

claim: The thermodynamic calculation suggests that the simulations resulting in 'Attached' shells would eventually reach completion on a longer timescale.
source: However, the thermodynamic calculation does suggest that the simulations resulting in 'Attached' shells would eventually reach completion on a longer timescale.
evidence: This is inferred from the thermodynamic model predictions.

claim: Assembly is most robust for the default cargo diameter (for which the model was parameterized), but productive assembly occurs for cargo diameters varied over a factor of four.
source: As shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2, assembly is most robust for our default cargo diameter (for which the model was parameterized), but productive assembly occurs for cargo diameters varied over a factor of four.
evidence: This is demonstrated through additional simulations shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: For εCC=1.6 the results with pre-equilibrated cargo are very similar to those obtained without pre-equilibrating the cargo.
source: For εCC=1.6 the results are very similar to those obtained without pre-equilibrating the cargo.
evidence: This is observed by comparing simulation results with different initial conditions.

claim: For εCC>1.6, successful assembly and detachment is limited to more narrow ranges of shell-shell and shell-cargo interaction strengths than in Figure 3, due to an increased prevalence of 'Attached' and 'Stalled' configurations.
source: However, for εCC>1.6, successful assembly and detachment is limited to more narrow ranges of shell-shell and shell-cargo interaction strengths than in Figure 3, due to an increased prevalence of 'Attached' and 'Stalled' configurations.
evidence: This is observed by comparing simulation results with pre-equilibrated cargo to Figure 3.

claim: 'Attached' and 'Stalled' configurations are particularly common for εCC=3, when the cargo forms a hexagonally close packed crystal which strongly resists deformation by shell protein assembly.
source: The latter are particularly common for εCC=3, when the cargo forms a hexagonally close packed crystal which strongly resists deformation by shell protein assembly.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: Moderate effective cargo-cargo interactions are most consistent with the observations of shell assembly and budding in carboxysome experiments.
source: Taken together, the results from both assembly protocols (Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2) suggest that moderate effective cargo-cargo interactions are most consistent with the observations of shell assembly and budding in Refs. (Cameron et al., 2013; Chen et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred by comparing simulation results to experimental observations.

claim: Moderate cargo-cargo interactions are strong enough to drive cargo globule formation, but malleable enough to allow shell assembly to deform and eventually sever intra-globule interactions.
source: Such interactions are strong enough to drive cargo globule formation, but malleable enough to allow shell assembly to deform and eventually sever intra-globule interactions.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: Studies of assembled carboxysomes report varying degrees of order for the encapsulated cargo, ranging from none to paracrystalline order.
source: Studies of assembled carboxysomes report varying degrees of order for the encapsulated cargo, ranging from none to paracrystalline order (Iancu et al., 2007; 2010; Kaneko et al., 2006; Schmid et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Below εCC<3 kBT, true fcc order of the encapsulated cargo is not observed.
source: Below εCC<3⁢kB⁢T, we do not observe true fcc order of the encapsulated cargo.
evidence: This is observed in the equilibrium simulations.

claim: For all parameters leading to significant filling, even those well below the cargo liquid-vapor transition, the cargo becomes organized in concentric layers.
source: However, for all parameters leading to significant filling, even those well below the cargo liquid-vapor transition, the cargo becomes organized in concentric layers (Figure 6).
evidence: This is observed in the equilibrium simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: Similar cargo organizations are observed within shells which have budded from cargo globules in dynamical simulations.
source: We observe similar cargo organizations within shells which have budded from cargo globules in dynamical simulations.
evidence: This is observed in the dynamical simulations.

claim: Ordering of the cargo does not require crystallinity of the initial globule.
source: These results demonstrate that ordering of the cargo does not require crystallinity of the initial globule.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing ordering even without initial crystallinity.

claim: The magnitude of ordering increases with cargo loading, but, for fixed loading, is essentially independent of the cargo-shell interaction strength εSC.
source: Moreover, the magnitude of ordering increases with cargo loading, but, for fixed loading, is essentially independent of the cargo-shell interaction strength εSC.
evidence: This is observed in the equilibrium simulations.

claim: Ordering is observed within filled shells due to confinement, even if εSC is set to 0.
source: We observe ordering within filled shells due to confinement, even if even if εSC is set to 0 (Figure 6—figure supplement 1), as previously noted by Iancu et al. (Iancu et al., 2007).
evidence: This is observed in the equilibrium simulations shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and supported by citation.

claim: The simulations show that assembly can proceed by two classes of pathways: (i) a multi-step process in which the cargo forms a dense globule, followed by adsorption, assembly, and budding of shell proteins, or (ii) single-step assembly, with simultaneous aggregation of cargo molecules and shell assembly.
source: Our simulations show that assembly can proceed by two classes of pathways: (i) a multi-step process in which the cargo forms a dense globule, followed by adsorption, assembly, and budding of shell proteins, or (ii) single-step assembly, with simultaneous aggregation of cargo molecules and shell assembly.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation results.

claim: The minimal interactions included in the model are sufficient to drive both classes of assembly pathways, suggesting that they are a generic feature of assembly around a fluid cargo.
source: This result demonstrates that the minimal interactions included in our model are sufficient to drive both classes of assembly pathways, suggesting that they are a generic feature of assembly around a fluid cargo.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: The model demonstrates that the same interactions which drive assembly of shells can also drive budding from and closure around an amorphous globule of cargo.
source: Moreover, while we cannot rule out the existence of active mechanisms in biological examples such as carboxysomes, our model demonstrates that the same interactions which drive assembly of shells can also drive budding from and closure around an amorphous globule of cargo.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation results.

claim: The decisive control parameter determining the assembly pathway is the cohesive energy between cargo molecules.
source: The decisive control parameter determining the assembly pathway is the cohesive energy between cargo molecules, which could arise through direct cargo-cargo interactions or be mediated by auxiliary proteins (Cameron et al., 2013).
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing different pathways for different cargo-cargo interaction strengths.

claim: Relatively weak cargo interactions lead to single-step assembly pathways, while stronger interactions favor formation of the cargo-shell globule.
source: Relatively weak cargo interactions lead to single-step assembly pathways, while stronger interactions favor formation of the cargo-shell globule.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation results.

claim: Strong shell-shell interactions cause assembly to proceed rapidly during globule formation, limiting the size of the globule.
source: Strong shell-shell interactions cause assembly to proceed rapidly during globule formation, limiting the size of the globule.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: If a large globule is already present, strong interactions tend to drive malformed assemblies.
source: Moreover, if a large globule is already present (e.g. due to time-dependent protein concentrations within a cell), strong interactions tend to drive malformed assemblies.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: An important functional difference between the two classes of assembly pathways is control over the amount of packaged cargo.
source: We find that an important functional difference between the two classes of assembly pathways is control over the amount of packaged cargo.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation results.

claim: The multi-step assembly pathways always generate a shell filled with cargo molecules.
source: While the multi-step assembly pathways always generate a shell filled with cargo molecules, shells assembling around a diffuse cargo can be tuned from nearly empty to completely full by controlling the strength of cargo-shell interactions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation results.

claim: Shells assembling around a diffuse cargo can be tuned from nearly empty to completely full by controlling the strength of cargo-shell interactions.
source: While the multi-step assembly pathways always generate a shell filled with cargo molecules, shells assembling around a diffuse cargo can be tuned from nearly empty to completely full by controlling the strength of cargo-shell interactions.
evidence: This is demonstrated through the simulation results.

claim: Recent works demonstrated that protein cargos can be targeted to BMCs via encapsulation peptides that mediate cargo-shell interactions.
source: Recent works demonstrated that protein cargos can be targeted to BMCs via encapsulation peptides that mediate cargo-shell interactions.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge from recent work.

claim: Packaged amounts of engineered cargo were much lower than for native core enzymes.
source: However, packaged amounts were much lower than for native core enzymes (Parsons et al., 2010; Choudhary et al., 2012; Lassila et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Both cargo-shell and cargo-cargo interactions (direct or mediated) must be controlled to assemble full shells.
source: Our simulations show that both cargo-shell and cargo-cargo interactions (direct or mediated) must be controlled to assemble full shells.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results.

claim: A general equilibrium theory describes the ranges of parameter values for which assembly occurs.
source: We also find that a general equilibrium theory describes the ranges of parameter values for which assembly occurs.
evidence: This is demonstrated by comparing the theoretical model to simulation results.

claim: At finite timescales, there is a rich variety of assembly morphologies.
source: However, the dynamical simulations demonstrate that, at finite timescales, there is a rich variety of assembly morphologies.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: This constraint is consistent with previous studies on viruses and other assembly systems, which found that formation of ordered states requires multiple, cooperative weak interactions between subunits.
source: This constraint is consistent with previous studies on viruses and other assembly systems, which found that formation of ordered states requires multiple, cooperative weak interactions between subunits (Hagan, 2014; Whitelam and Jack, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Assembly is least robust to parameter variations when the cargo crystallizes before shell assembly.
source: We find that assembly is least robust to parameter variations when the cargo crystallizes before shell assembly.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: The assembling shell is unable to deform or penetrate the cargo complex when the cargo crystallizes, leading to defect-riddled, non-budded complexes.
source: The assembling shell is unable to deform or penetrate the cargo complex, leading to defect-riddled, non-budded complexes.
evidence: This is observed in the simulation results.

claim: Within the limits of the simplified model, procarboxysome complexes are at least partially fluid prior to successful shell assembly.
source: Within the limits of our simplified model, this observation suggests that procarboxysome complexes are at least partially fluid prior to successful shell assembly.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing that crystalline cargo inhibits assembly.

claim: Observations of ordered cargo within assembled shells may be explained by packing constraints.
source: Moreover, we find that observations of ordered cargo within assembled shells may be explained by packing constraints.
evidence: This is inferred from the simulation results showing ordering due to confinement.

claim: BMCs contain many more hexamers (formed from multiple protein sequences) than the model and thus must include a greater range of hexamer-hexamer interactions.
source: In reality BMCs contain many more hexamers (formed from multiple protein sequences) and thus must include a greater range of hexamer-hexamer interactions.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the model based on knowledge of BMC structure.

claim: In the case of assembly around vapor-phase cargo, the size of the assembling shell will be primarily dictated by the preferred shell protein curvature and thus relatively uniform.
source: We speculate that in the case of assembly around vapor-phase cargo, the size of the assembling shell will be primarily dictated by the preferred shell protein curvature and thus relatively uniform.
evidence: This is speculation based on the simulation results.

claim: During assembly around a condensed globule, the shell protein interactions could be strained to accommodate a globule which is larger or smaller than the preferred curvature, causing the shell size to depend on a complex balance of intermolecular interaction strengths and variables such as the local RuBisCO concentration.
source: However, during assembly around a condensed globule, the shell protein interactions could be strained to accommodate a globule which is larger or smaller than the preferred curvature, causing the shell size to depend on a complex balance of intermolecular interaction strengths and variables such as the local RuBisCO concentration.
evidence: This is speculation based on the simulation results.

claim: The model is minimal, intended to elucidate general principles of assembly around a fluid cargo, and thus may apply to diverse systems including prokaryotic microcompartments, viruses, and engineered delivery vehicles.
source: Our model is minimal, intended to elucidate general principles of assembly around a fluid cargo, and thus may apply to diverse systems including prokaryotic microcompartments, viruses, and engineered delivery vehicles.
evidence: This is a statement about the scope and applicability of the model.

claim: The predicted trends for how assembly mechanisms and morphologies vary with control parameters can be experimentally tested by microscopy experiments.
source: The predicted trends for how assembly mechanisms and morphologies vary with control parameters can be experimentally tested by microscopy experiments.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experimental work.

claim: Testing will be most straightforward in vitro, where subunit-subunit interactions can be tuned by varying solution conditions and the stoichiometries of shell and cargo species can be readily varied.
source: Such testing will be most straightforward in vitro (e.g. Luque et al., 2014; Douglas and Young, 1998; Rurup et al., 2014; Patterson et al., 2014; Patterson et al., 2012; Zhu et al., 2014; Rhee et al., 2011; Rurup et al., 2014; Wörsdörfer et al., 2012), where subunit-subunit interactions can be tuned by varying solution conditions and the stoichiometries of shell and cargo species can be readily varied.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experimental work with citations to relevant in vitro systems.

claim: The findings can be tested in vivo by mutations which alter known protein binding interfaces, or by altering expression levels of RuBisCO or carboxysome proteins.
source: While there is currently no BMC assembly system starting from purified components, our findings can be tested in vivo by mutations which alter known protein binding interfaces, or by altering expression levels of RuBisCO or carboxysome proteins.
evidence: This is a suggestion for future experimental work.

claim: The model can serve as a qualitative guide for understanding how multicomponent complexes assemble in natural systems, or to reengineer them for new applications.
